#  Pittsburgh’s Best Restaurants: The 26 spots that reflect how we eat in the region right now 
Alexandra Wimley/Post-Gazette 
#  Pittsburgh’s Best Restaurants: The 26 spots that reflect how we eat in the region right now 
This list, presented alphabetically in two sections, reflects the full scope of dining in Pittsburgh in 2026. It spans genres, price points and neighborhoods, and highlights the diverse traditions and perspectives that shape how we eat in the region right now.
Some restaurants are rooted in heritage, others in innovation, and many draw strength from a personal blend of the two.
I’ve broken out a Top 10 this year, listed alphabetically, followed by the Best of the Rest. This is a first in more than a decade of writing Best Restaurants lists for the Post-Gazette and other publications.
Advertisement
Each of these restaurants — and many others — were visited at least once over the past 12 months, often more. The most important qualification: Is it delicious?
Hal B. Klein
Here’s how dining critic Hal B. Klein reported Best Restaurants
Want to know about the rest of the process for determining the list? Check out the explainer for the nitty-gritty details.
Pittsburgh has marched through serious setbacks and losses, including the devastatingly long tail of the COVID-19 pandemic, to a moment when an extraordinary group of restaurants is once again commanding national attention.
My hope is that, the next time you're deciding where to eat, you’ll return to this roster of 26 standouts.
Advertisement
Fueling each one are chefs, bartenders, servers, owners, dishwashers and farmers who have invested years of dedication to build the skill sets that create dining experiences worth celebrating. This list is a recognition of their hard work.
Get eating, Pittsburgh.
* * *
* * *
## The top 10
* * *
* * *
## Apteka
Eastern European/vegan
(Sophia Lucente/For the Post-Gazette)
Apteka is a rare restaurant that stays at the top of the conversation by holding true to its identity even as it keeps evolving. The 10-year-old mainstay remains anchored in a plant-based expression of Eastern European cooking while embracing, ever more deeply, the yields of the region’s growers and foragers.
Hal B. Klein
Pittsburgh’s best quick-serve restaurants of the year
The synthesis has allowed chefs and co-owners Kate Lasky and Tomasz Skowronski to steadily expand their menu from the (still excellent) pierogi and snacks that first brought them attention to a bevy of rotating dishes that speak to Western Pennsylvania in the mid-2020s. Components that can seem simple are the product of layered techniques such as fermentation, smoking, simmering and roasting.
Apteka’s dessert program has followed the same arc over the decade, rising from a little bonus at the end of the meal into a reason to visit just for an indulgent treat. (Peak-hour lines persist, but you can almost always slip in toward the close of service and land a table or a seat at the bar.) Lasky and Skowronski spin seeds and nuts into concoctions every bit as creamy and luxurious as anything with a dairy base, and the kitchen’s jams and preserves give yeasted sweet breads zing and pop.
The work has earned the pair multiple James Beard Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic nominations, including a finalist nod in 2023. This year, Apteka made the long list for the national James Beard Award for Outstanding Wine and Other Beverages Program, recognition for an innovative lineup of hard-to-find wines (a feat in Pennsylvania) and drinks, with and without alcohol, built on house-made tinctures and cordials.
_4606 Penn Ave., Bloomfield;aptekapgh.com_
* * *
## Bar Marco
Seasonal Italian
(Giuseppe LoPiccolo/Post-Gazette)
The maturation of Bar Marco is one of my favorite stories. The restaurant opened just as I started writing about food and drink in Pittsburgh, and it’s been a treat to watch it grow into one of the city’s smartest dining destinations while holding on to the energetic, noble hospitality mission it was founded to foster. Bar Marco in 2026 is a vibrant, modern spot with timeless appeal.
Owner Justin Steel, kitchen manager Matt Woods and company handle seasonal produce with a distinctly Italian philosophy of letting the best possible ingredients star in tandem with just a few other items also at their peak.
A meal at the end of August glowed with bright summer flavors.
Take the mafalde with pesto. The long, wavy noodles meant to resemble the lacy frills of early 20th-century aristocracy — scratch-made, like all the pasta here — wore a classic pesto (prime basil, new-season garlic) along with green beans just coming in. Branzino, crisp and fresh, mingled with summer squash and fava beans. Tomato and peaches, both hitting their stride, made a standout starter.
You’ll find similarly of-the-moment dishes throughout the year, as well as Italian staples such as rigatoni dressed in famed cookbook author Marcella Hazan’s buttery tomato sauce.
Bar Marco was among the first in Pittsburgh to focus on minimal-intervention winemakers, and its ever-changing list still reflects that style. The cocktail program — a pillar since the beginning — remains strong, and the beers, while limited, are terrific.
Bar Marco switched to a service-included model in 2015: The price you see on the menu is what you pay when you’re done, tax and service included. More restaurants should be doing this.
There are just 35 seats, so making a reservation is a wise move.
_2216 Penn Ave., Strip District;barmarcopgh.com_
* * *
## Chengdu Gourmet
Sichuan Chinese
(Alexandra Wimley/Post-Gazette)
Wei Zhu ushered Pittsburgh into an era of outstanding regional Chinese cooking when he opened Chengdu Gourmet in a subterranean space on Forward Avenue in Squirrel Hill in 2014. He had already spent nearly a decade in local kitchens, but that was his moment to push forward the bold flavors of his home city, Chengdu, China.
Now 60, Zhu is a six-time James Beard Award Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic semifinalist who operates two Chengdu Gourmet locations. The Squirrel Hill restaurant is the more intimate of the pair, while his dining room in Ross, opened in 2022, has a sprawling, celebratory feel. Both feature tables outfitted with turntables for big groups (the ideal way to experience Chengdu Gourmet), and Chengdu 2 adds a couple of private rooms for even larger parties (my favorite way to dine there).
Sichuan cuisine is one of the eight great culinary traditions of China (where countless regional variations also exist). It’s best known for málà, the combination of red-hot chili pepper and Sichuan peppercorn (the numbing dried fruit of the prickly ash tree), and you’ll find that pairing throughout the menu in signature dishes such as cumin lamb and mapo tofu. Zhu also embraces the refined fare of the ancient city, which at various points in history served as the capital or summer residence of kingdoms.
I tend to eat at Chengdu 2 more often than at the original, but the menus are much alike, and Zhu bounces back and forth between the two so quickly he seems to have installed a teleportation device.
_5840 Forward Ave., Squirrel Hill; 4768 McKnight Road, Rosschengdugourmetpa.com_
* * *
## Dish Osteria
Southern Italian
(Giuseppe LoPiccolo/Post-Gazette)
Walk into Dish Osteria and Bar on a busy night and you’ll immediately wonder whether you’ve crashed a perpetual party. The front bar is packed, the dining room is shoulder to shoulder and greetings fly from table to table as guests make their way inside.
At times, everyone seems to be one degree of separation from the table beside them.
Executive chef and co-owner Michele Savoia has made Dish one of Pittsburgh’s most dependable restaurants for more than two decades, building fierce loyalty through warm hospitality and a kitchen that almost never misses its mark. Drawing on his Sicilian roots, he balances longtime signature dishes with seasonal plates that give regulars a reason to return, while assuring first-timers they’ve landed in the perfect place for dinner.
Seafood has always been one of the menu’s strengths, and the house-made pastas remain among the city’s best. Order the daily soup, too; it’s a sure thing. Fill the table with starters. Feast through dessert.
The bartenders are as welcoming as the servers, and the back bar holds one of the deepest collections of digestivi in town. By the time dinner winds down, you’ll understand why so many people in the room seem to know each other. Dish has a way of making even a newcomer feel like a regular.
_128 S. 17th St., South Side;dishosteria.com_
* * *
## Duo’s
Mexican
(Giuseppe LoPiccolo/Post-Gazette)
It took Pittsburgh a few years to grasp that Duo’s isn’t a canteen for Duolingo employees, even though it is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Pittsburgh-headquartered technology company. I’m happy to see that more diners are now realizing what many of us have known since it graduated from a takeout taco window to full-service, sit-down dining in 2023: Duo’s is the best upscale Mexican restaurant in Western Pennsylvania (and, in my opinion, well beyond).
Executive chef Marcella Ogrodnik and her team remain rooted in the art of transforming dried heirloom corn into nutritious and flavorful masa-based dishes. But she has also broadened her repertoire to include showstoppers such as Yucatan-influenced hamachi pescado roasted in banana leaf with orange mojo verde, lusty smoked goat birria born in Jalisco and spicy-citrusy aguachiles that draw on coastal Mexico’s long tradition of absorbing Japanese culinary techniques.
Duo’s introduced Friday, Saturday and Sunday brunch service this year, reviving early-days favorites such as suadero tacos and debuting new items such as crispy, fluffy masa pancakes that may make you reconsider everything you thought you knew about flapjacks. Ogrodnik pays homage to her Salvadoran heritage with a full breakfast plate from the Central American nation.
Heather Perkins, one of Pittsburgh’s foremost front-of-house personalities, joined the staff this year as general manager, tightening hospitality and systems.
_5906 Penn Ave., East Liberty;duos-pgh.com_
* * *
## Fet-Fisk
Nordic/farmer-focused
(Alexandra Wimley/Post-Gazette)
Fet-Fisk has settled over the past year from a new sensation into a destination restaurant. (It earned Pittsburgh’s first James Beard Award Best New Restaurant finalist nod in 2024, among other national accolades.) Founders Nik Forsberg and Sarah LaPonte have maintained the creative zest of their earliest pop-ups while deepening the expertise needed to steer the restaurant into its mature era.
Forsberg’s Nordic-meets-Appalachian menu runs heavy on seasonal set changes but now also has anchors, such as roasted chicken and mussels, that you’ll want to order each time (with top-notch french fries). Seafood lovers will rejoice at the varied selection of raw, pickled and roasted dishes, and vegetarians always have something to look forward to at Fet-Fisk.
The dimly lit bar is one of the city’s most romantic spaces and a fun spot to catch up with friends; it’s the kind of room that seems bound to produce grizzled, cool regulars who, years from now, will tell stories about what Bloomfield was like in the ’20s.
Fet-Fisk keeps things interesting with its beverage program: cocktails rotating through flavor profiles (earthy, bitter, etc.), a strong wine list shaped by natural and biodynamic growers, and chuggable beers and nonalcoholic drinks.
The dining room, now expanded, is a better choice for larger groups and a more mellow, though still joyful, experience. Service here is on-point — it’s chill but polished.
_4786 Liberty Ave., Bloomfield;fetfisk.net_
* * *
## Lilith
Coastal Contemporary
(Justin Guido/For the Post-Gazette)
Dining at Lilith is a radiant experience. It all feels effortless, which is a testament to the behind-the-scenes hard work of co-owners Jamilka Borges and Diane DeStefano and their staff.
Borges, now a three-time James Beard Award semifinalist, orchestrates the savory side of the menu, grounding it in top-quality ingredients, with a large portion coming from the region’s best farmers. The layering is often so sly that you might think you could replicate the results at home. You almost certainly wouldn’t come close; she and her team coax out flavors with a command that comes from years spent building perfect bites.
Sure, panzanella is usually a workaday picnic dish, but this summer’s version, stacked with various melons, grains, crisp lettuce, house-made bread and just enough tomatoes (whose concentrated flavor escaped the blowout from August’s rains) was a treat worth paying for.
Smart technique keeps other dishes singing: handmade spaghetti with deep, peak-season tomato sauce, energized by earthy chanterelles and pops of grilled corn, or a pork chop with giant beans, sharpened by acidity and sweetened by Jimmy Nardello peppers.
DeStefano runs pastry and baking. You’ll meet her work first in the city’s best complimentary bread service: high-hydration focaccia spiked with rosemary, served with creamy ricotta and grassy olive oil. That craft resurfaces throughout the meal in other forms — from airy croutons in the panzanella to the pan sobao in a tuna tartare given an almost tataki quality by infused chive oil.
Pace yourself (or at least pretend to), because you’ll want at least two desserts. DeStefano is a baked Alaska savant, so order one of those, then go wild card on another, or several.
The floor team is just as feel-good, keeping things breezy while holding fast to the proper steps of service, such as making sure your water glass is never empty. The space is as lovely as the food.
Borges and DeStefano deserve extra praise for training a new generation of women in Pittsburgh’s hospitality industry. That investment leaves Lilith with a strong bench as the two near the opening of their second restaurant, Giulia in Bloomfield.
_238 Spahr St., Shadyside;lilithpgh.com_
* * *
## Morcilla
Spanish
(Sophia Lucente/For the Post-Gazette)
Morcilla’s menu draws heavily on Spain’s Basque region, with a good pinch of Western Pennsylvania seasonality folded in. Fixtures include the big-plate chicken dish arroz con pitu de caleya and Laurel Hill Farm trout with salsa verde and artichokes, and when there’s something to celebrate, you must visit the Lawrenceville spot for the smoked beef short rib with horseradish labneh.
It’s always wise to order a spread of small plates, too. Keep an eye on the scallops, salads and soups, which change as the months turn.
Veteran bar manager Lynn Falk runs one of the most detailed beverage programs in Pittsburgh. Make a habit of stopping in for an aperitif and a snack whenever you happen to spot open seats at the bar while you’re in Lawrenceville.
Morcilla has matured into such a seamless operation that its founders left town a few months ago and all but the most loyal regulars likely didn’t notice.
While Justin Severino and Hilary Prescott Severino retain ownership stakes, the restaurant is now firmly in the hands of its executive chef and co-owner, Nate Hobart. He oversees a dedicated staff whose members, person for person, are among the longest-tenured in the city.
All of it adds up to a dining experience that is consistently in Pittsburgh’s top tier.
_3519 Butler St., Lawrenceville;morcillapittsburgh.com_
* * *
## Pusadee’s Garden
Thai
(Justin Guido/For the Post-Gazette)
Pusadee’s Garden is still overwhelmingly popular; landing a reservation is nearly as tough now as it was when it reopened in 2021. I worried that such sustained success might eventually lull the upscale Thai restaurant into a more conservative autopilot mode.
An August dinner settled those concerns.
Head chef Bootsaba “Gik” Tongdee (a 2024 James Beard Award Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic semifinalist) and her crew are pressing ahead to offer a growing lineup of the most transportive dishes in Pittsburgh.
As befits a place so in demand, there is a roster of staples such as lamb shank and potatoes in massaman curry (a fork-tender journey into a dreamscape) and pan-roasted halibut with tamarind and chili garlic sauce (crisp-skinned juiciness dressed in soured savoriness), yet even those are more nuanced now than they were a year ago.
Other standbys leave room for seasonality — I’m thinking of the peak-summer version of the morning glory, bok choy and mushroom stir-fry, intense with wok hei and including fruity, foraged chanterelles.
Many of the newer orders follow the calendar, too. This summer’s vibrant som tum phon la mai blended high-season sweet corn with warm-weather fruits, snappy green beans, toasted peanuts and a good dose of fish sauce.
Pusadee’s Garden’s design remains as striking as it was five years ago: a series of connected dining rooms of various sizes, a glass-enclosed jewel-box bar mixing sharp cocktails, a showpiece entryway and an open kitchen. Tucked inside it all is the modern courtyard garden, which deepens the sense of escape whenever the weather allows.
Although reservations are hard to come by, don’t hesitate to try for a walk-in. Pusadee’s holds back a good number of tables to reward spontaneity and, generally speaking, the wait won’t be too long. If you do need to kill some time, head across the street for a drink at the always delightful Allegheny Wine Mixer.
_5319 Butler St., Lawrenceville;pusadeesgarden.com_
* * *
## Siempre Algo
Modern American
(Giuseppe LoPiccolo/Post-Gazette)
Siempre Algo’s rise to excellence is one of the most impressive feats I’ve watched in my years on this beat. Brian Hammond kicked off upscale dining in East Allegheny in 2018 with a restaurant built around sustainability, but its output often felt a couple steps shy of brilliance.
He, along with executive chef Chris Castine, found their voice in that philosophy over the past two years. The name may translate to “there’s always something,” and the kitchen may frequently switch up dishes, but the output is anything but “whatever is on hand is just fine.”
In fact, it’s spectacular.
Still, Siempre Algo was the hardest restaurant for me to place on this list. The meals I had there in September and October were, start-to-finish, the strongest of the reporting window. Yet there are design elements — especially the continued insistence on using squares of QR code menu printed off-center on cheap paper and dining room lighting too dim even for romance backgrounded with a reflective glare from a very bright, open kitchen — that made me think twice about putting it in the Top 10.
In the end, the bold play toward adventurousness and curiosity in Castine’s kitchen won out.
Plates run from a light, easy compressed melon and Jinhua ham salad brightened with pepper-ginger vinaigrette and mint to heftier fare such as house-made smoked beef and lamb sausage with saffron risotto. Along the way come modern nods to heritage Pittsburgh food culture, including a pierogi stroganoff filled with pastrami, potatoes and herbs and served with shiitake mushroom and veal demi-glace.
They also turn out a deep roster of vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free dishes that delight every bit as much as anything else on the menu.
Service is sharp, as is the bar program. Hammond’s commitment to the well-being of his staff, including paid time off and robust healthcare benefits, are an example I’d like to see more restaurant owners follow.
For me, that offsets some of the other annoyances. Nevertheless, I’d love to see printed menus or, at the very least, as much thought in how the QR code is presented as goes into all the other details at this exceptional restaurant.
_414 E. Ohio St., East Allegheny;siemprealgopgh.com_

## THE REST OF THE BEST
* * *
* * *
## Eleven Contemporary Kitchen
Contemporary American
(Justin Guido/For the Post-Gazette)
Eleven is the multi-tool of upscale Pittsburgh restaurants: It’s utterly dependable, surprisingly versatile and always there to fix what ails you. The Strip District spot made a splash when it opened in 2004 and hasn’t lost a step in the 22 years since.
Eleven set the foundation for our modern upscale dining era, bridging the gap between an older-school style and, as its name implies, something more contemporary. Its roster of alumni has wide tendencies, influencing the culinary and service systems (as well as a good number of local food producers). For all this, Eleven has a place of its own as a bridge to the rest of this year’s Best Restaurants list.
That dependability starts with continuity. Eli Wahl took the helm as executive chef a decade ago, making him just the third person to run the kitchen. His contemporary American menu mixes enduring classics such as a best-in-class chicken entree, standards whose sides change a few times a year and a handful of specials.
There’s an enticing option for everyone from the conservative diner who knows what they like to eaters eager to try something new. The space is just as adaptable, with nooks for anniversary dinners, long tables for a post-business-meeting meal and the Tavern for a hang with pals.
That breezy side of the house is first come, first seated (you’ll want a reservation for the main dining room). It serves the same menu and tacks on a second with treats such as the iconic Eleven burger and soft pretzels built on a bagel-like dough, then finished in a deep fryer, yet still pliable and free of oily residue. Look for happy hour deals, too.
1150 Smallman St., Strip District; elevenck.com
## Amazing Dumplings
Northern Chinese
(Justin Guido/For the Post-Gazette)
Amazing Dumplings is about as literal as a restaurant name gets, and the signature items at this Squirrel Hill standout live up to their top billing.
Co-owner Fenping Geng makes every dumpling skin from scratch, and it’s been a pleasure to watch her artistry grow over the years. The ever-ebullient Geng folds and rolls dough tinted with a medley of house-made vegetable dyes into fantastical patterns that delight the eye moments before we demolish plate after plate of them.
She’s also a gracious host, and service here is warm and upbeat.
Her husband, chef and co-owner Feng Gao, draws most of his inspiration for the fillings from the traditional repertoire of China’s northern Shaanxi and Heilongjiang provinces and Ningxia autonomous region. He also leaps into the contemporary canon with General Gao’s and tropical prawn combinations. A vinegar-based dipping sauce accompanies most dumplings, while others, including the standout hot-oil spicy sesame version, get their own kitchen-made accoutrements.
Gao’s Xi’an-style hand-pulled noodles warrant at least one order, and probably more. His tomato and egg over wide biangbiang distills the best of Chinese comfort food, and the beef and chopped-pepper versions, doused in sizzling oil, are slippery, fiery thrills.
Round out the meal with a couple of starters, such as the gossamer scallion pancakes and refreshing cucumber salad.
Bring a group or make it a point to visit regularly. Or do both.
_5882 Forbes Ave., Squirrel Hill;amazingdumplings.com_
* * *
## Balvanera
Argentine
(Hal B. Klein/Post-Gazette)
Aspinwall native Meredith Boyle and her Argentina-born husband, Fernando Navas, took a calculated leap when they decided to open a bigger version of their New York City restaurant in 2023. Their faith that Pittsburgh would embrace a sophisticated take on Argentine cuisine has paid off handsomely, with crowds filling the cosmopolitan Strip District dining room nearly every night it is open.
Balvanera gets the essentials right: It’s polished; you can stop in for an affordable snack and a well-made drink or settle in for a lavish meal; and the service lets you enjoy the people you’re with and worry about nothing else.
Navas’ menu reaches beyond steakhouse fare (though the steaks are there, too) into the wider repertoire of a country whose cuisine blends European influences with Indigenous foodways (and here, an accent of Western Pennsylvania produce).
Omnivores should home in on the house-made sausages — my favorite is rueda de cordero, lamb with pear chutney and an herby salad, but you’ll be happy with whatever you choose — and the whole table will want seasonal salads and small plates such as arancini de coliflor.
Pastry chef Ginger Fisher Baldwin is a wizard of the confectionery kitchen. Balvanera is one of those places where you really must plan to order several desserts.
The couple closed their New York location earlier this year to focus wholly on Pittsburgh; they have a new Downtown restaurant in the works.
_1660 Smallman St., Strip District;balvanerarestaurants.com_
* * *
## Cafe Momentum
Mission-driven American
(Hal B. Klein/Post-Gazette)
Dallas-based Cafe Momentum brought its model to Pittsburgh a little more than three years ago, offering paid, hands-on training across front- and back-of-house to rolling cohorts of 15- to 19-year-olds impacted by the criminal justice system. The Downtown location was the organization’s second in the country (it has since expanded to Atlanta and Denver) and has given mentorship and wraparound support to nearly 200 youths since its inception.
Laudable enough as is, but Cafe Momentum wouldn’t earn a place on this list if not for the work of chef de cuisine Robert “RC” Carter and his team.
Lunch in the comfortable, bright dining room is easygoing, with virtuous salads and house-made seitan sausage sharing a menu with hearty hamburgers and macaroni and cheese.
Dinner brings larger-format dishes including rack of lamb, potato-crusted salmon and Momentum’s signature smoked and fried chicken with mashed potato, collard greens, buttermilk biscuit and black pepper gravy.
_268 Forbes Ave., Downtown;cafemomentum.org/restaurant/pittsburgh_
* * *
## Casbah
Mediterranean
(Sophia Lucente/For the Post-Gazette)
Regulars — and there are so many of them — flock to Casbah weekly or more for beloved menu staples (there are many of them, too), including scratch-made pastas, beautiful braised lamb shoulder with hummus and a double-cut pork chop with prosciutto risotto. While those favorites draw longtime and first-time guests alike, the Mediterranean-influenced kitchen often works in seasonal specials that deserve your attention, too.
This Shadyside stalwart was well ahead of the curve on local sourcing, something that wasn’t happening much around town when it opened in the mid-1990s. It hasn’t let up since.
Service reflects big Burrito Restaurant Group’s 30-plus years of developing Pittsburgh’s top hospitality talent, front and back of house. The cocktail program offers spins on classics that don’t stray far from the originals, and the bar sports a thoroughly curated wine list leaning heavily on California and Western European vintners.
_229 S. Highland Ave., Shadyside;casbah.kitchen_
* * *
## EYV
Vegetable-focused Modern American
(Sophia Lucente/For the Post-Gazette)
Michael Godlewski seems to have figured out the formula for getting Pittsburgh to eat its vegetables: a reasonably priced three-course prix fixe menu ($50 as of press time) that celebrates the bounty of Western Pennsylvania agriculture through the lens of a chef who cares about the small details on the plate.
Every meal begins with a trio of snack-sized bites — crunchy broccoli “chicharrones” with beer cheese and crisp hummus fritters are regulars, and the closer on a summer visit was an earthy masa tart set off by Old Bay-spiked custard, pickled celery and seaweed caviar. From there, the menu unfolds with a midsize dish and then an entree. Aside from a cabbage pastrami (really!), the rest is highly seasonal.
Desserts and extra courses are available as add-ons. I found the tomato French toast a playful showcase for a summer savory staple.
EYV has a strong bar program and friendly service. The upstairs seating in the double-decker dining room is more intimate, though the ground floor offers a view of Godlewski working in the open kitchen.
_424 E. Ohio St., East Allegheny;eyvrestaurant.com_
* * *
## F&F Pizzeria
Pizza/Italian
(Giuseppe LoPiccolo/Post-Gazette)
I remember feeling a mix of excitement and skepticism when I learned Frank Falcinelli and Frank Castronovo were bringing an offshoot of their lauded Brooklyn pizzeria to Mt. Lebanon. Did Pittsburgh really need an outsider coming into an already burgeoning pizza destination?
Were we being used as a testing ground for a potential chain?
I’m glad the optimist in me won out. The Franks, along with business partners Anthony Simasek and Robert Mullin, both of whom have Pittsburgh ties, launched something special, and the region is the better for it.
The pizzas — 12- and 18-inch pies, plus slices at the bar — are among the very best we have, with a deep char on the well-fermented crust. F&F’s classics, from the textbook-terrific cheese to the ocean-kissed white clam, can be transcendent, and most of the combinations carry just enough pizzazz without tipping out of balance.
What lifts F&F into the rafters (and onto this list) is its completeness as a full-service restaurant. The concise kitchen menu covers Italian staples such as crisp arancini and plush meatballs, and there are always big salads built on locally grown ingredients.
The pastas are as tip-top as the pizza. Vodka rigatoni stracciatella is a must-order, and you’ll be lucky if spinach and herb gnudi is in rotation the night you visit; the dumpling’s tender semolina and ricotta shell melts into the grassy, well-seasoned filling.
F&F is family friendly, too.
_307 Beverly Road, Mt. Lebanon;fnfpizzeria.com/location/pittsburgh_
* * *
## Fig & Ash
Contemporary American
(Justin Guido/For the Post-Gazette)
Fig & Ash has found its focus again in 2026, six years into its run as one of the keystone restaurants on the North Side’s East Ohio Street.
Executive chef and co-owner Cory Hughes’ menu is a fairly settled blend of New American cooking, all properly executed and much of it from the wood-burning hearth. Hughes and his team allow just enough seasonal and micro-seasonal change to keep things lively.
It’s become one of those places where you can count on your favorite dish a couple of times a year and still find a reason to return for what’s new.
Or split the difference. Order a fixture such as heirloom carrots with honey-whipped ricotta, Marcona almond and sage brown butter alongside a more fleeting delight: buttery black cod with charred onion puree, late-spring fiddlehead ferns, briny artichokes and lemon-thyme cream spiked with funky miso to bring lift and umami.
I’d expect recent additions to become standards, too, among them sous chef Mike Bickel’s roast chicken, crisp, tender and airy beneath a mustard-based Carolina barbecue glaze.
The dining room is inviting, the service attentive and the beverage program excellent across the board.
_514 E. Ohio St., East Allegheny;figandashpgh.com_
* * *
## Jillian’s Restaurant
Farm-to-table American
(Justin Guido/For the Post-Gazette)
I’m convinced that a table at Jillian’s would be one of the hardest reservations to score in Pittsburgh if it were in the city rather than on a side street deep in New Kensington. I’m also convinced the unexpected address is part of its charm.
Chef and co-owner Phil Call runs the region’s most dedicated farm-, forest- and ranch-to-table operation. On any given night, up to 100% of the menu features ingredients produced in Pennsylvania or nearby Ohio. A few local restaurants experimented with whole-animal butchery a decade ago; Call keeps the practice alive in his small kitchen.
Lest you think that’s code for “cheffy,” stop by Wednesday burger night, when Call turns the trim from special order sides of cow into a hamburger so beefy it would give Peter Luger’s famous creation a run for its money (and price point). He spikes Heinz ketchup with house-made fermented hot peppers, a brilliant move that brings sly balance to the condiment.
The bar program is limited but wonderful. Pair your meal with a spicy pickled martini that a pal who works in the industry declared “the best martini I’ve ever had.” Service and the room are more casual than the check might suggest, and that suits Jillian’s.
_400 Freeport St., New Kensington;jillians-restaurant.com_
* * *
## Kiku
Japanese
(Giuseppe LoPiccolo/Post-Gazette)
Make a plan to claim one of the 7 seats at Kiku’s sushi bar. There, you can have an omakase experience that will, from time to time, reach the peak of the form at about half the price of pristine counters elsewhere.
Pittsburgh’s oldest Japanese restaurant is deep into a revival, thanks in part to new business from Nippon Steel’s arrival in the region, in part to diners rediscovering a Station Square mainstay that dates to 1983 and in part to loyal customers who never forgot it.
One of Kiku’s original sushi chefs, Takuharu Okumura, remains a presence. Now, however, Makiko Hatori, who purchased the restaurant from its founding owners five years ago, typically works alongside Yasuko Balsomico and Saya Shimizu; it’s rare anywhere to see a sushi bar run by three women and it’s something Kiku should be proud of.
The rest of the menu is enticing, too. Much as the design reflects its first owners’ vision, the hot kitchen tilts toward classic Japanese cookery, with highlights including cold udon noodles, sukiyaki and shabu-shabu. Beef tataki, seared rare, and tuna tataki salad with sesame seeds, greens and basil pesto are enthralling.
_225 W. Station Square Drive, South Side;kikupittsburgh.net_
* * *
## One by Spork
Modern American tasting menu
(Matt Freed/Post-Gazette)
Two years ago, Chris Frangiadis decided it was time to embark on the final chapter of his long and successful career as a chef in Pittsburgh, Kansas City and the U.S. Virgin Islands by reimagining Spork, the Bloomfield restaurant where he’d been partner and executive chef since 2018.
He and business partner Andrew Tepper reopened the establishment as One by Spork, a fine dining, tasting-menu-only concept in which up to 16 guests sit together at a semicircular round table as Frangiadis, general manager and beverage director Cecil Usher and a cast of staff who share front- and back-of-house duties present a parade of dishes and beverage pairings a la theater in the round.
Frangiadis, a 2020 James Beard nominee for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic, uses classic cooking techniques, timeless fermentation methods and a laboratory of modernist technology to build the dishes, which are centered around the restaurant’s adjacent farmette and the highest quality ingredients from regional purveyors. Those dishes change fairly frequently.
Usher, now a partner in the project, pairs each course with a wine and cocktails – or a separate nonalcoholic pairing, which is as good as the boozy one. Many of the cocktails and n/a drinks are prepared with the same ingredients and science lab used by the kitchen.
At $275 plus tax and tip as of press time, it’s a splurge. But for those who can swing it, One offers an experience unlike anything else in Pittsburgh.
_5430 Penn Ave., Bloomfield;onebyspork.com_
* * *
## Ramen King 
Northern and Central Chinese
(Hal B. Klein/Post-Gazette)
The hand-pulled and knife-sliced noodles that co-owner and noodle king Fu Li Zhang turns out all day at Ramen King 2 are a revelation to anyone who hasn’t experienced the chew of a fresh strand or the way it laps up flavor. Zhang is currently in China, but plans to return in early 2027 with new recipes. He and co-owner Nan “Long” Zhang, who goes by Alan, have trained noodle makers working at #2, near the Ross Park Mall, as well as the Canonsburg original.
Both locations serve noodle combinations that arrive in soups built on long-simmered bases of beef and chicken stock which will have you reveling in the warmth of five-spice. If you’re lucky enough to see it on the menu that day, an opaque lamb broth infused with white pepper and star anise is as perfect vessel for the springy strands of wheat. I craved both for weeks afterward. More noodles land in northern Chinese stir-fries, and you also should get at least one order of those if you’re with a big group.
(If you’re wondering whether this is the place for Japanese ramen, it isn’t. The name reflects the Chinese origin of the noodles, known as lāmiàn.)
Alan Zhang’s mother, Guiyiang “Sister” Man, is the head pastry chef. She’s based primarily at theCanonsburg location but mentors chefs at the Ross restaurant. Her dumplings, bao and sandwiches from the bread kitchen could earn Ramen King a spot on this list without a single noodle.
_#1: 3351 Washington Rd., Canonsburg_  
  
 _#2: 3400 McIntyre Square Drive, McCandless_
## Senti
Northern Italian
(Lucy Schaly/Post-Gazette)
Every meal at Senti leaves me thinking I should become more of a regular. The northern Italian restaurant is one of the classiest in town, yet it often gets overlooked in a category crowded with flashier dining rooms. Do yourself a favor and make a reservation as soon as you finish reading this.
Owner Franco Braccia’s half century in hospitality shows in the way he engages every table from the second guests step inside until the moment they leave. He’s an easy conversationalist leading a well-trained staff that minds every small detail.
Longtime executive chef Antonio Garcia’s cooking grows more compelling year by year. There are classics such as arancini and fried artichokes, house-made pastas galore and salads that shift a little, or a lot, with the seasons. This is the kind of establishment where individual main courses make sense; family-style-always person that I am, I found myself having a tough time sharing the branzino steamed tender in parchment with onion, cherry tomatoes, white wine, lemon and parsley.
Senti’s wine program is phenomenal.
_3473 Butler St., Lawrenceville;sentirestaurant.com_
* * *
## Titusz
Eastern European
(Hal B. Klein/Post-Gazette)
As a general rule, a restaurant should be open for at least a year before I name it a Best Restaurant. Rarely, a newcomer is so evocative that it persuades me to bend it.
Such is the case with Titusz.
Few openings in the past decade have moved me the way Csilla Thackray’s homage to her Central European roots does.
Thackray, executive chef and co-owner, digs deep into the traditions of Hungarian and Austrian kitchens with a curated menu that combines heritage staples with hyper-seasonal hits. Her cooking is a reminder of how elegant eastern Continental cuisine can be, much of it plated at Titusz in vivid color.
The personalized beauty of Titusz extends to smallest design details, from embossed menus printed on sturdy stock to lovingly framed photographs of Thackray’s family history.
Beverage director Sean Rosenkrans, Thakray’s spouse and general manager of Allegheny Wine Mixer, assembled a brilliant roster of Austrian and Hungarian wines you’ll be hard-pressed to find anywhere else in Pennsylvania, as well as a stunning after-dinner drinks list. The bar staff whips up a riot of original cocktails, and service, led by general manager Robert Chaffin, carries the assurance of a long-established house.
_4129 Butler St., Lawrenceville;tituszpgh.com_
* * *
## Udipi Cafe
Vegetarian Indian
(Hal B. Klein/Post-Gazette)
The region’s longest-running vegetarian restaurant remains one of its most vital. Manjunath Sherigar opened Udipi Cafe in 1996 to serve worshipers at Sri Venkateswara Temple — one of the oldest traditional Hindu temples in the United States — and feed the growing community of Indian immigrants working in a city just emerging as a technology hub. It also, naturally, became a magnet for vegetarians of every stripe, who had few options at the time.
The dining room is casually chaotic and full of life, the service quite friendly. On any given night, you’ll find a diverse spectrum of Pittsburgh, from large groups to couples deep in private conversation amid the hubbub, all working through a menu of South Indian specialties and a few pan-Indian favorites.
Udipi drew early and ongoing attention for its dosa, and the crispy, stuffed crepes made from fermented grain and pulse batters continue to shine. Still, you ought to venture beyond them. It took me until a visit this summer to order vegetable pulav, a wickedly nourishing, warmly spiced rice stew full of root vegetables, lentils, peas and beans and topped with roasted nuts. This might be my new pick-me-up.
_4141 Old William Penn Highway, Monroevillefacebook.com/pages/Udipi-Cafe/_
* * *
## The Vandal
Contemporary American
(Alexandra Wimley/Post-Gazette)
The Vandal stands out among Pittsburgh bistros for its youthful energy, evident in both its clientele and its enthusiasm for outstanding service. It draws on a Western European tradition of restaurants where small, elegant bites meet easy hospitality to foster intimate evenings.
Tea lights and soft overhead bulbs give the dining room, which seats about 30, a romantic glow. Don’t save it just for courtship, though.
Co-owner Joey Hilty’s menu has taken on a more classic bistro character over the past few years, with smart salads (if you’ve read this far, you’ve probably realized how much I love a well-composed salad) and market-driven small plates.
Entrees are French-influenced and change fairly often, so don’t grow too attached to a favorite. Do, however, pay attention to whatever pasta is on the menu; every one I’ve had in recent years has been terrific.
The well-curated wine list favors small natural and biodynamic producers, and the cocktail program is a treat. I dig the after-dinner drinks list, too.
_4306 Butler St., Lawrenceville;thevandalpgh.com_

Labs & Groups - Robotics Institute Carnegie Mellon University
# Labs & Groups
Advanced Agent - Robotics Technology Lab
Katia Sycara
Researchers explore multi-agent planning and scheduling, multi-agent learning, multi-agent negotiation, and decision support for human teams. 
AIIRA
AI Institute for Resilient Agriculture 
AirLab
Sebastian Scherer
The AIR lab develops and tests perception and planning algorithms for unmanned air vehicles. 
ARCS Lab
Jiaoyang Li
Autonomous agents accomplishing collaborative tasks intelligently in dynamic environments. 
Atkeson Lab
Chris Atkeson
Current research focus is enabling robots to learn strategies to do tasks from direct instruction, googling and using the web, observation, and practice via reinforcement learning. 
Auton Lab
Artur W. Dubrawski, Jeff Schneider
We build practical large-scale deployments of very highly autonomous self-improving systems. 
Biomedical Image Guidance
John Galeotti
Our research into the guidance of biomedical tools applies novel optics and computer vision algorithms to the design and real-time analysis of biomedical imaging modalities such as OCT and ultrasound. 
Biorobotics Lab
Howie Choset, Matthew J. Travers
The Biorobotics Lab reduces complicated high-dimensional problems found in robotics to low-dimensional simpler ones for design, analysis, and planning. 
Bot Intelligence Group
Jean Hyaejin Oh
The main theme of research in Bot Intelligence Group (BIG) is to develop robotic intelligence ranging from the low-level autonomy to the high-level cognitive abilities. 
CMU Center for Autonomous Vehicle Research
Deva Kannan Ramanan, John M. Dolan
The center performs fundamental research on advanced perception and next-generation decision-making algorithms that will enable vehicles to perceive and navigate autonomously in diverse real-world conditions. 
CMU Safe AI Lab
Ding Zhao
Aims to develop reliable, explainable, verifiable, and good-for-all artificial intelligence. 
Cognitive Assistance Laboratory
Kris M. Kitani
Research to assist everyday life by fully utilizing the power of AI 
Computational Behavior (CUBE) Lab
Laszlo A. Jeni
The CUBE Lab focuses broadly on multi-modal methods for computational behavior science, specifically in areas of modeling, analysis, and synthesis of human behavior and emotion using diverse sensors. 
Computational Imaging at CMU
Ioannis Gkioulekas, John Galeotti, Matthew O'Toole, Srinivasa G. Narasimhan
Computational imaging, illumination, display, light transport, microscopy, and more. 
Computer Vision @ CMU
The community of researchers doing Computer Vision @ CMU. 
Connecting Language to Actions & the World (CLAW) Lab
Yonatan Bisk
The lab is run by Yonatan Bisk and is housed primarily in the Language Technologies Institute, but includes members from both the ML Department and the Robotics Institute. 
CREATE Lab
Illah Nourbakhsh
The CMU CREATE Lab is dedicated to utilizing technology and collaboration to tackle societal concerns, including environmental awareness, enhancing classroom learning, fostering emotional well-being in children, and visualizing global and local narratives 
Deep Robot Optical Perception (DROP) Lab
The DROP Lab’s research goal is to develop robotic systems capable of operating in complex dynamic environments. 
DeLight
Dong Huang
We develop perception solutions, advance deep learning with light-weight approaches, and deploy light-weight algorithms to embedded platforms. 
Dexterous Manipulation and Soft Robotics Lab
Nancy Pollard
Foam hands seek to bridge the gap in realized dexterity between soft robotics and classical rigid robot hands. 
Driverless Intelligent Vehicles Lab
John M. Dolan
The DRIVE Lab performs research on behaviors, planning, control, and perception for autonomous vehicles with a focus on adversarial multi-agent systems. 
FARM Lab
George A. Kantor, Abhisesh Silwal
Field Autonomy and Robotic Manipulation for agriculture, forestry and more. 
Generative Intelligence Lab
Jun-Yan Zhu
Collaboration between Human Creators and Generative AI Models 
Graphics Lab
Jessica K. Hodgins
The Carnegie Mellon Graphics Lab conducts cutting-edge research on computer graphics and computer vision, integrating insights from computer science, robotics, and mechanical engineering. 
Human And Robot Partners Lab
Henny Admoni
Our goal is to understand and develop autonomous, intelligent robots that help people live better. 
Human Sensing Lab
Fernando De la Torre Frade
The goal of the Human Sensing Lab is to develop new machine learning algorithms to model and understand human behavior from sensory data. 
Illumination and Imaging Lab
Srinivasa G. Narasimhan
The Illumination and Imaging (ILIM) Laboratory at the Robotics Institute is dedicated to the study of light transport and the development of novel illumination and imaging technologies. 
Intelligent Autonomous Manipulation (IAM) Lab
Oliver Kroemer
Explore the challenges of creating general purpose robots that are capable of performing manipulation tasks in unstructured and everyday environments. 
Intelligent Control Lab
Changliu Liu
Our focus is building intelligent and autonomous robots that think, behave and interact with the world in the way that human beings do, so they can better serve, assist and collaborate with people. 
Intelligent Coordination and Logistics Laboratory
Stephen Smith
Developing new theories, techniques and software technologies in planning, scheduling and control. 
Intent Robotics Lab
Andrea Bajcsy
The goal of the Interactive and Trustworthy Robotics Lab is to enable embodied AI agents to reliably interact with the open world. 
LeCAR Lab
Guanya Shi
Exploring the intersection of machine learning and control theory. 
Legged Systems Group
Hartmut Geyer
Research focuses on legged systems: Principles of legged dynamics and control, their relation to human motor control, and rehabilitation technology. 
MattLab
Matthew J. Travers
Multi-Modal Perception Uber Good 
MetaMobility Lab
Inseung Kang
Dedicated to pioneering cutting-edge wearables, robotics, and AI technologies that transcend traditional human physical capabilities, aiming to redefine the boundaries of human mobility. 
Microdynamic Systems Laboratory
Ralph Hollis
Exploring the limits of robotics in terms of speed, precision, dexterity and miniaturization. 
Momentum Lab
Jeffrey Ichnowski
Our research spans soft robotics, computer vision, machine learning, and multi-agent systems. 
Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Lab
Eni Halilaj
Our ultimate goal is to integrate insights from our experimental and computational work to develop effective rehabilitation strategies aimed at restoring and preserving pain-free mobility. 
Navlab
Martial Hebert, Christoph Mertz
CMU Navigation Laboratory 
Pathak Research Group
Deepak Pathak
Artificial Intelligence at the intersection of Computer Vision, Machine Learning & Robotics 
Physical Perception Lab
Shubham Tulsiani
Developing learning mechanisms to explore fundamental problems in computer vision and robot manipulation. 
Reliable Autonomous Systems Lab
Reid Simmons
We are developing reliable, highly autonomous systems (especially mobile robots) that operate in rich, uncertain environments. 
Resilient Intelligent Systems Lab
Wennie Tabib
Resilient autonomy and agile flight in complex, unstructured environments. 
Robot Perception Lab
Michael Kaess
The Robot Perception Lab performs research related to localization, mapping and state estimation for autonomous mobile robots. 
Robotic Caregiving and Human Interaction Lab
Zackory Erickson
Our research aims at enabling intelligent physical human-robot interaction. 
Robotic Exploration Lab
Zachary Manchester
The Robotic Exploration Lab conducts research in control, motion planning, and navigation for robotic systems that explore our planet and our universe. 
Robotics Academy
The Robotics Academy is committed to using the motivational effects of robotics to excite students about science and technology. 
Robots Perceiving and Doing Lab
David Held
We develop new methods for robotic perception and control to allow robots to operate in the messy, cluttered environments of our daily lives doing research at the intersection of robotics, machine learning, and computer vision. 
Search-based Planning Laboratory
Maxim Likhachev
Our goal is to develop planners that work in real-time and deal with complex real-world environments. 
SHRED Lab (Social Haptics Robotics and Education Laboratory)
Melisa Orta Martinez
Making haptics and robotics to improve Education and Wellbeing. 
Soft Machines Lab
Carmel Majidi
Soft Machines Lab creates integrated soft materials for human compatible machines and electronics. 
Surgical Mechatronics Laboratory
Cameron Riviere
We are developing intelligent tools for microsurgery and minimally invasive surgery. 
TBD Lab
Aaron Steinfeld
Transportation, Bots, & Disability Lab Supporting seamless transportation and interaction with robots 
Textiles Lab
James McCann
The Carnegie Mellon Textiles Lab extends the state of the art in textile design and fabrication. We seek to collaborate broadly both inside and outside the Carnegie Mellon community. 
Visualization and Image Analysis
George D. Stetten
We are developing new methods of displaying, analyzing, and haptically rendering images, primarily for medical applications. 
Zhang Lab
Ji Zhang
SLAM, navigation, planning, scene understanding and exploration. 
Zoom Lab
Zeynep Temel
Compliant Systems for Mechanical Intelligence

The Carnegie Mellon University Navigation Laboratory group builds computer-controlled vehicles for automated and assisted driving. Since 1984, we have built a series of robot cars, vans, SUVs, and buses. More recent research expands to smart infrastructure, focusing on machine vision application and affordable sensors.
The CMU Center for Autonomous Vehicle Research website is an up-to-date source of information on CMU’s self-driving car research.
The video below features some highlights from 1984 through 2007, but leaves out many of the Navlab platforms.

SECTION 3. - SUBMISSION OF COST CENTER OBJECT LEVEL BUDGET.

The County Director of Budget and Finance shall submit to the County Controller the cost
center object level budget for each of the above line item appropriations by December 31, 2025.

SECTION 4. - USE OF GENERALLY ACCEPTED ACCOUNTING PRINCIPLES.
Expenses incurred and revenues received for conducting the public business of Allegheny
County and meeting the debt charges shall be recorded by the County Controller in accordance

with General Accepted Accounting Principles as related to the operation of State and local
governments.

SECTION 5. - ADHERENCE TO APPLICABLE LEGAL REQUIREMENTS.

All expenses made pursuant to the adopted 2026 Operating Budget shall adhere to
requirements set forth in the Home Rule Charter, the Administrative Code of Allegheny County,
and where applicable, the Second Class County Code.

SECTION 6. - AVAILABILITY OF FINANCIAL RECORDS FOR INSPECTION.

All agencies receiving appropriations from the County shall make their financial records
open at reasonable times to the visitation, inspection, and examination by duly authorized officers,
inspectors, and accountants of the County.

SECTION 7. — LINE ITEM DETAIL DELIVERY.

The line item detail of the adopted appropriations shall be delivered to the County
Executive within three (3) days of this adoption.

SECTION 8. — TRANSFERS.

Transfers made between line items and departments shall be made in accordance with
Chapter 805 of the Administrative Code of Allegheny County.


SECTION 9. — MODIFICATION TO CURRENT COUNTY DEPARTMENTAL
STRUCTURE.

County Council approves the following modifications within the existing structure of
Allegheny County Government:

1. The Department of Budget and Finance is renamed the Department of Management and
Budget (hereinafter “DMB”).

2. The Department of Equity and Inclusion is abolished and moved under the supervision
and of DMB and shall be known as the Division of Business Inclusion.

3. The Division of Purchasing is moved under the supervision of DMB.

SECTION 10. — SEVERABILITY.

If any provision of this Resolution shall be determined to be unlawful, invalid,
void or unenforceable, then that provision shall be considered severable from the
remaining provisions of this Resolution which shall be in full force and effect.

SECTION 11. - REPEALER.

Any Resolution or Ordinance or part thereof conflicting with the provisions of
this Resolution is hereby repealed so far as the same affects this Resolution.


SECTION 11. - EFFECTIVE DATE.

This Resolution shall become effective upon its approval.

# A Guide to Market Square
Located in the heart of Downtown Pittsburgh, Market Square is a must-see for tourists and locals alike. Market Square is surrounded by shops and restaurants and boasts year-round activities in the center of the space. Discover Market Square's rich history.
Credit |
Dnapps Production
## What is Market Square?
Market Square is was originally constructed in Downtown Pittsburgh in 1764 and become home to the area’s first courthouse, jail and newspaper. In 2009, the area went through a renovation that focused on catering to pedestrians by offering a variety of restaurants and dining options, shopping, activities, accommodations and year-round programming. Then in 2026, Market Square reopened after a $15 million redesign that included a glass canopy, more walkable sidewalks, expanded outdoor dining spaces, and more trees and greenery.  

Credit |
Dnapps Productions
## Restaurants in Market Square
Tap into the history of Market Square by visiting Nicholas Coffee & Tea Co., an institution since 1919 or the iconic Primanti Bros., serving the ultimate Pittsburgh sandwich stacked with french fries and coleslaw since 1933. 
Pizzaiolo Primo serves handmade pizzas and pasta, No. 1 Sushi Sushi presents fresh rolls for the lunch crowd, Medi's on Market lets you build your own bowls and if you’re looking for craft beer, City Works Eatery & Pour House has over 90 selections on tap.
Stop into The Boredom Set for a coffee or quick bite for lunch before heading out for the day. Looking for a sweet treat? Be sure to check out Millie's Homemade Ice Cream using only local and real ingredients to bring you delicious and flavorful ice cream, including vegan and dairy-free options!  

Many of the Market Square restaurants turn into a hub for nightlife, including Las Velas, which turns into one of the best dancing destinations in the city during the weekends. Emerson's is the perfect spot for cocktails and Instagramable moments, and Space Bar brings the intergalactic right into the heart of our city with innovative drinks to fit the theme.
## Shopping & More
There are plenty of great, local businesses to stop and shop at in and around Market Square.
Boutique La Passerelle is must-visit store featuring European fashion with a Pittsburgh flair, and 306 Forbes Boutique offers women's fashion, accessories and state-of-the-art microblading, permanent lip and eye makeup. For the guys, be sure to visit Heinz Healey's, a locally-owned and operated Pittsburgh men’s clothier for 33 years carrying high-end fashion. Sports fans, stop into DK Pittsburgh Sports for Steelers, Penguins and Pirates merch that make perfect gifts, and stick around to meet the owner!
If you're ready for some pampering, you'll want to make an appointment at one of the salon and spas in Market Square. The Health Club & Spa at the Fairmont Pittsburgh is a great option for a full-service spa menu ranging from massages to a variety of full-body treatments. And, for the more athletic crowd, Moxie Mind & Body is a Pilates studio with private, duet and group classes.   

## Market Square for the Holidays
You'll definitely want to experience Market Square during the holidays as it turns into an incredibly festive Winter Wonderland! The Peoples Gas Holiday Market™, inspired by the original German Christkindlmarkts (or "Christmas Market"), brings a cherished European tradition to Pittsburgh. 
With an international flair and local charm, the market features shops from around the world with Asian, African, Haitian and Latin American goods. You can also find Santa's House and plenty of helper elves around an illuminated market square for a unique family-friendly photo op.
Across the way from the square is The Rink at PPG Place, an outdoor ice skating rink complete with a stunning 65-foot illuminated Holiday tree in the center.  

The 2025 Peoples Gas Holiday Market opened Nov. 22 and runs through Dec. 24, giving you plenty of time to shop! The weekend before Thanksgiving hosts Highmark Light Up Night, which dazzles by lighting the Christmas Tree downtown along with musical acts, firework displays, shopping, food and so much more.
**_VENUE CHANGE: With construction in Market Square, the2025 Peoples Gas Holiday Market has been moved to the Cultural District._**
## Market Square Farmers Market
Events and activities are happening around Market Square year-round. From May-Oct. on Thursdays from 10 a.m.-2 p.m., visitors and locals can experience the Market Square Farmers Market featuring a wide range of local vendors and live performances during Thursday lunch hours. 
During the summer months, Market Square transforms into an outdoor yoga studio for Yoga in the Square programming, offering free classes to the public on Tuesdays and Sunday. And, the Friday and Saturday Night Market brings together local businesses and the community for a fun pop-up shopping event from June-Oct.
Market Square Farmers Market
## Market Square Parking
There is limited street parking available in the area surrounding Market Square in Downtown Pittsburgh. Visitors can park in the Market Square Garage managed by the Alco Parking Corporation or explore real-time parking availability via ParkPGH. 
## Things to Do Nearby
The best part about being in Market Square is that you in a central of hub of Pittsburgh fun, with great things to do in every direction and just a short walk away. Head south from Market Square to PPG Place (one minute walk), a gorgeous plaza with stunning fountains during the warmer months and a gigantic Christmas tree and ice skating rink in cooler months.  

To the west, Point State Park is where our three rivers come together in a beautiful park with iconic fountain, and also where hikers and bikers frequent as they see the best of our city. Follow Market Square north and you'll be on our 6th Street Corridor, full of a diverse collection of some of Downtown's best restaurants. To the east (and a touch south), you'll enter our Cultural District, our bustling arts district with 14-square-blocks of world-class theaters, exhibits and galleries.

# Downtown Draws: Exploring Cafes, Cocktail Bars, Jazz Joints & Other Enticing Stages
Excited crowds will soon descend upon downtown Pittsburgh for the NFL Draft in late April, but there’s plenty brewing to check out before then. Whether you’re coming for the cultural offerings, new culinary finds or an unexpected moment of restoration, we’ve got some ideas to brighten even the palest of winter days.
Start the morning at the newest downtown location of Ruckus Cafe, where you can cozy into a corner nook with two armchairs, next to a selection of CDs and vinyls playing on rotation. Fuel up with a latte, smoothie (featuring flavors like coco mango and acai blueberry), bagel sandwich, fresh-made salad or toasted sandwich (featuring avo chicken, crunchy veggies and so on). Recently, Ruckus excitedly announced they’d earned a Silver designation as a Sustainable Pittsburgh Restaurant — an identification that recognizes their commitment to our community, economy and planet. (This means that by visiting, you too can feel good about supporting an environmentally responsible practice.)  
  
Other small businesses have recently opened downtown as well, like Origin Story Coffee and Confleurtti, in the lead-up to the ongoing modernization of Market Square (projected for spring) and the planned Arts Landing park.
Rendering for Arts Landing, scheduled to open in June 2026
Credit |
Renderings by Field Operations
Just a few minute-walk away from Ruckus Cafe, those looking for a pampering pause might consider booking a treatment at the Fairmont Pittsburgh Spa, a third-floor oasis that gets flooded with light even on a gray-streaked day. Their signature scent brings calming energy from the moment you step off the elevator, allowing you to sink into your mini-escape high above the urban bustle. Choose between decadent offerings from customized facials to Thai massages, with optional enhancements ranging from CBD to hot stone. All treatments include use of the sauna and steamroom. (Day passes to use their facilities are available, too.)  
  
Afterward, you can continue to unwind with lunch enjoyed in the spa’s soothing lounge, or grab a bite one floor below in the fl.2 bistro (one of the few spots that’s open downtown at lunchtime on Mondays). Inside an inspired space dreamed up by Barcelona-based designer Lázaro Rosa-Violán, Chef Fernando Canales leans into Mexican and Asian influences with his dishes (think filet mignon served with mole sauce, for example). At lunchtime, enjoy selections from French onion soup and Caesar salad to sweet potato flatbreads and lobster rolls.  
  
If you land in the Fairmont’s bustling property later on in the day, take advantage of the bar’s Social Hour (from 4 to 6, Mondays through Fridays) for discounted bites, cocktails, wine and beer. (Keep an eye out for upcoming events at the hotel as well, like a Mix & Mingle: Galentine’s Edition Cocktail Class taking place on February 12.)
The evening hours downtown bring a bounty of arts-centric happenings, all within a couple-block radius. Before seeing a show at one of the city’s many venues, grab a hearty meal at Meat and Potatoes, tapas at Barcelona Wine Bar or scrumptious sushi rolls at Gi-Jin (fine dining) or The Warren (more casual, but delicious nonetheless).
Then check out thoughtful programming at August Wilson African American Cultural Center, a variety of events (from weekly salsa dancing to Edinburgh Fringe Festival acts) at Greer Cabaret Theater or stimulating performances at O'Reilly Theater, such as An Enemy of the People (which runs from February 4 through 22).
The latest Pittsburgh Cultural Trust spectacle to land on the scene — Wicked — will play at the Benedum Center through Sunday, February 15. The Broadway-turned-movie-sensation returns to the stage here for a mesmerizing rendition of this imaginative glimpse into what happened in the Land of Oz. Glinda and Elphaba captivate audiences from the get-go with their talent and wit. And while the storyline and musical numbers (“Defying Gravity,” we’re looking at you…!) prove as captivating as ever, this particular production features impressive special effects, lighting work and acrobatics that give some lucky actors the chance to “fly.” This gives the audience the chance to temporarily suspend their disbelief and sink into the magic, too.  
  
In attending one of the opening nights, we found that several of the lines felt especially poignant in this moment in time we find ourselves navigating. It also seemed particularly therapeutic to sit in community with other enraptured theater goers, as collective laughter (and sometimes sniffles) filled the grand space downtown.   
  
The whole experience proved an alluring escape, as the auditorium filled with a warming green glow, at several points silhouetting the glamorous wigs of dazzling guests in front of us who had dressed the part in glittery pink and green gowns. (Neighboring audience members snapped selfies with them at intermission, to the delight of everyone looking on.) The whole night had the electric buzz of seeing a show on Broadway, with theater attendants even helping the flow of traffic in the women’s restrooms during intermission.
Zoe Jensen as Glinda and Jessie Davidson as Elphaba in the National Tour of WICKED
Credit |
Joan Marcus
Before or after the show, stop into centrally located jazz hub-restaurant-bar Con Alma, which launched a campaign in December to help keep its doors open in the midst of some financial troubles. As Pittsburgh’s only jazz club — and the only nightlife for live music downtown — Co-owner and Music Curator John Shannon says they believe that Pittsburgh is a better place because Con Alma exists. They know the jazz community here needs a home. (A Fundraising Gala on Sunday, February 1, will be hosted by local comedy hero Bill Crawford and showcase live jazz led by Orrin Evans).  
  
“When you walk into Con Alma you realize that Pittsburgh is indeed a jazz city,” he explains. “You are taken with the warm atmosphere and the sounds of jazz. The freshest cocktails and unique cuisine complement the experience of your senses.” The menu features “Latin American cuisine with soul,” and the charming ambiance includes no TV screens — only live jazz and vinyl records spinning, with the walls showcasing black-and white photos that celebrate this city’s 50s golden jazz era.
Credit |
Aaron Jack
Another welcoming venue for cocktails nearby, Space Bar, opens its doors to all. Owner Dale Vaughn explains the aim of their gathering place in Market Square, which shows off “molecular mixology” that translates to innovative drinks with clever monikers like the Espresso Mars-tini, Waffle Crisp Gold Fashioned and Starship (gin, lime and house tonic, served with dry ice).   
  
“We want to transport people to a hopeful future,” he says, “to imagine a time when humanity gets past wars and xenophobia, when we go to the stars.” At Space Bar, they host monthly events like Drag Bingo, Space Trivia and other LGBT community events. On the horizon: a new menu debuts in March, and they’re hosting the USBG Northeast cocktail competition in May.  
  
Vaughn continues, “We welcome people onto the observation deck of the SS Oasis, a warm, comfortable, sleek starship with cocktails that might be reminiscent of Earth, but alien enough for the adventurers inside all of us.” In the midst of these cold and dark days, we certainly love the sound of such open-armed and creative hospitality.

## Con Alma
Enjoy food with soul at Con Alma, Downtown Pittsburgh's newest hot spot for dinner and brunch. Live jazz featuring local musicians accompanies some of the best food and drinks in the city, including a Latin-inspired menu paired with classic cocktails from the prohibition era.
## The Speckled Egg
Sometimes, the best way to spend a Sunday morning is treating yourself to a delicious pile of French toast. When that craving hits, The Speckled Egg is there for you. The upscale diner has menu items such as brown butter French toast, the goat omelette, and a full cocktail menu. If waffles are more your thing, see #13, further down this list. 
> View this post on Instagram
> A post shared by Karen | PGH Foodie (@karen.hoang)
## Gaucho Parrilla Argentina
Another popular downtown eatery is Gaucho Parrilla Argentina. The restaurant, which specializes in sandwiches and wood-fired meat, moved downtown a while back to accommodate their growing foodie fan base.  

## Nicky's Thai Kitchen
Look no further than Nicky's Thai Kitchen for the best Thai food in town. They have a lengthy menu to fit all tastes, and you can typically find dinner specials on their website. Plus, customers can choose between the bar or BYOB.
## Ritual House
Ritual House was inspired by world travels and a passion for Pittsburgh. Captivating art, devilish details, and luxurious comfort are just the start of the experience. This is our love letter to Pittsburgh — a way to add to the magic of our hometown. We invite you to make Ritual House your sanctuary, and create your own rituals — whether that’s toasting major moments or gathering with people you love — here, in our house.  

## The Original Oyster House
For a tried-and-true Pittsburgh tradition, head to The Original Oyster House, the oldest bar and restaurant in the city. There, you'll enjoy tasty fried seafood and tavern drinks right inside a historic landmark.
## Sienna Mercato
Sienna Mercato is a 3-story Italian food "marketplace" in Pittsburgh's historic Cultural District, each floor with its own distinct dining destination. Emporio, on the bottom floor, specializes in meatballs, whereas Mezzo, on the second floor, has a small wine bar and an extensive menu of classic and creative Italian dishes, including artisanal pizzas, Italian cheeses, charcuterie, and more. Il Tetto, the top floor, boasts city skyline views and a beer and wine garden that can be enjoyed year round, thanks to the retractable glass ceiling.

## Bridges and Bourbon
For "dining done differently," modernistic cocktails that are visually stunning and food that engages the senses, head to Bridges and Bourbon. The sophisticated yet social atmosphere makes this the perfect spot to celebrate a special occasion or date night. 
## The Commoner and Biergarten
The Commoner is Pittsburgh's modern American tavern, and it is anything but ordinary. It specializes in American classics with a touch of the unexpected. During the summer season, the restaurant's rooftop open-air Biergarten is open Thursday through Saturday evenings. It's the perfect spot for happy hours or weekend meet-ups with friends. 
## Bakersfield
Craving tacos and tequila? Head to Bakersfield for authentic Mexican street fare and over 100 tequilas and whiskeys. This is the place to go for simple food and an upbeat atmosphere set against a backdrop of the finest country-western music. 
## Waffles, INCaffeinated
At Waffles, INCaffeinated, you can sample "exquisitely wicked" delicious waffles, both savory and sweet, creative sandwiches, and custom coffee drinks. Bring your family and friends along for this affordable and unique boutique dining experience in downtown Pittsburgh. 
## gi-jin
Sushi, hand rolls, and gin inspire this playful name that delivers big flavor through a refined Japanese approach to sushi. At gi-jin, Chef de Cuisine Michael Taylor serves up fresh, delicious nigiri, sashimi, and hand rolls, as well as sake, junmai, and cocktails to expertly pair with each flavor.
## fl.2
Luxury is stitched into every detail from the moment you walk into fl.2 at Fairmont Pittsburgh. From the upscale décor furnished by local makers to the house-made menu items focused on surprising combinations, fl.2 is perfect for corporate meetings and date nights and has family-sized portions for sharing.
## Rib Room
Prime rib fans, rejoice! This spot, tucked behind Meat and Potatoes in the Cultural District, focuses on prime rib aged in-house and perfectly cooked. Enjoy their supper club vibe in an upscale dining experience that seats only 16 per evening. Enjoy craft cocktails and an extensive whiskey list, sample wagyu carpaccio and lobster thermidor starters, and end your meal with the showcase Baked Alaska for Two.
## Whiskey B's
New on Market Square, dive into Whiskey B's menu! Fire up your palate with starters that range from bone marrow and turkey leg to fries, Brussels, and pickles, then dig in to delicious burgers, sandwiches, salads, and more, making this a perfect lunch or dinner spot.
## Sally Ann's
Acclaimed executive chef Jamilka Borges brings her creativity and flair to Sally Ann's, the casual dining experience open from breakfast to late night Downtown. Sip an espresso as you play classic arcade games, pick up sandwiches for lunch, or end your day with fresh-made pies and cakes at Sally Ann's.
## Del Frisco's Double Eagle Steakhouse
The restored Union Trust Building, on the corner of Fifth and William Penn Place, is home to Downtown's steakhouse. The two-story restaurant offers chef-driven cuisine, award-winning wine lists, craft cocktails, and live music nightly.
## Alihan's Coffee & Breakfast
If you love the amazing cuisine and friendly atmosphere of Downtown staple Alihan's, you're in luck! Located right next door, Alihan's Coffee & Breakfast offers Turkish Mediterranean breakfast, brunch, and lunch options. Try their takes on waffles, crepes, and French toast, or branch out and go for their specialty items like the Turkish Breakfast for Two, menemen (a mix of sautéed diced tomatoes and green peppers with eggs), and savory breakfast poğaça.
## Alta Via
If you love their Fox Chapel location, you'll be happy to know the same great flavors of Alta Via are now available Downtown! Located in the heart of PPG Place and steps from Market Square, enjoy elevated modern Italian fare from pumpkin and sage ravioli to squid ink fettuccini and so much more.

> A post shared by Alta Via (@altaviapgh)
## Fig & Ash
Fig & Ash offers modern American flavors with classic European influences and delicious home-away-from-home scratch cooking. They butcher their own meats, grind their own grains, and work with local farmers to create one-of-a-kind menu experiences.
## Dinner and a Show
Are you in town for a musical, symphony, or other excellent live theatre performance at the Cultural District? Fantastic dining options surround you within easy walking distance of our theatres. Consider the following streets, and remember to make reservations in advance:
  * **Sixth Street -** Restaurants line both sides of the street and extend into outdoor patios, making this a foodie heaven. International cuisine at gi-jin (Japanese), Alihan's (Mediterranean), and Cafe Milano (Italian) join American favorites Sally Ann's, Redbeard's, Olive Or Twist, and Giovanni's (home of the pickle pizza).
  * **Penn Avenue -** When you exit the Theatre Square Garage for a show, great restaurants are to your left and right. Gaucho Parilla Argentina, Con Alma, Rib Room, and Meat & Potatoes are closest to the major theatres, but it's also worth a farther walk down to Nicky's Thai Kitchen or Bridges & Bourbon as well.
  * **Liberty Avenue -** The next block down from Penn also has some local favorites. Grab a giant slice from Pizza Parma or the usual from Mike & Tony's Gyros, or go upscale at the flavor-packed Bae Bae's Kitchen.
  * **Strawberry Way -** One of the best walks in the city is to park at the US Steel Building and walk down the pedestrian-only Strawberry Way, enjoying the mural that encompasses each step. A fantastic sit-down dinner at The Commoner or the best hot dog in the city at Wiener World make this walk perfect.

Who are we?
Butcher and the Rye is Richard DeShantz Restaurant Group's whiskey-forward flagship in the heart of Downtown Pittsburgh's Cultural District, built around a reverence for dry-aged meats, old-world technique, and an unhurried evening at the table.
What is Butcher and the Rye best known for?
We're best known as Pittsburgh's whiskey destination. Our Whiskey Wall showcases 600+ bottles, and we're the first Pittsburgh bar ever nominated for a James Beard Foundation Award for Outstanding Bar Program. Pair that with rustic American plates built to stand up to a good pour.
What is the bourbon and whiskey program like at Butcher and the Rye?
Our whiskey list runs 600+ deep, from everyday pours to rare 10-, 12-, and 20-year flights, alongside barrel-aged cocktails, a Sazerac built the right way, and rotating cocktails on draft at the second-floor Rye Bar. If you're searching for the best bourbon bar in Pittsburgh, this is it.

# Pittsburgh Comedy Shows for Bridge Heat
Homestead By Manny Garavito Jul 10, 2026 8 min read 14 upcoming shows

Notify me 
✅ You're on the list!
The national mood right now is heat wave math. Everybody is calculating how far they are from air conditioning, how much water they should have had yesterday, and whether walking three blocks counts as an outdoor activity. Pittsburgh got the local version too, with extreme heat warnings around the holiday stretch and a July calendar that refuses to sit still.
That is very Pittsburgh. The city can be sweating through the bridges one minute, then turning around and getting ready for Picklesburgh, vintage cars, riverfront crowds, and a comedy lineup that looks like somebody let the whole group chat book a theater season.
## Pittsburgh summer is not subtle
Pittsburgh in July has three rivers, yellow bridges, festival crowds, and the kind of humidity that makes a folding fan feel like technology. You can either fight that all night or you can lean into the correct indoor plan: sit down, cool off, and let a comic do the sweating.
The Pittsburgh-area comedy run is loaded. Pittsburgh Improv in Homestead is doing heavy lifting, while PPG Paints Arena, Citizens Live at The Wylie, and Carnegie Music Hall of Oakland bring in the bigger theater nights. That gives you options, which is good, because one size does not fit every Yinzer evening.
